Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 names the owners of ground inside the town, resident or not — its entry 110 is Alexander Wolcott, who had been dead since 25 October 1830 — so this row bounds what this person was assessed for and says nothing about where the person was. tools/assert_tax_roll_ruling.py holds that ruling on the two readings it rests on. What no source states is that the man on the roll is the person on this card: data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json joins them on a name, by its rule “one resident of the surname 'Johnson' agrees with the entry's forenames; 4 bearer(s) of the surname were considered.”, and forenames agree initial for initial: entry 'Seth Johnson' against resident 'Seth Johnson'. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the town's own paper carries this name by 1 July 1835; whether the man it names was standing in the town is a claim this record cannot make, and present_on_scene_date says `uncertain` for that reason. No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Johnson, Seth” (tax_1833_051, line 103). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Johnson' agrees with the entry's forenames; 4 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). THE 1840 FEDERAL CENSUS — A HEAD FIVE YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1840 federal census of Chicago, read line by line off the left sheets in this repository, carries 1 head of this name — “Seth Johnson” (33S7-9YYJ-B3, printed page 226, line 7). This project has ruled the head a CANDIDATE and no more: the name agrees and is unique on both sides, but the reader graded the name on the sheet low, and a low-confidence read caps at a candidate however well the name agrees. A candidate is not an identity — nothing is asserted from it, no household of 1840 is carried back, and the ruling is recorded so that a reader can see it was made rather than missed. Under the rule that decided it (L6a low_confidence_caps_at_candidate), by the crosswalk's own ladder (data/research/census_1840/resident_crosswalk.json). LATER EVIDENCE ONLY. The ratified grading ladder binds: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to the 1835-07-01 scene. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and an 1840 head is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

back_projection.note: REFUSED, AND THE REFUSAL IS THE RECORD. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 prints an address against this name in 1843 and this pass will not carry it back to 1835. The 1835 record prints no trade for this person, so there is no 1835 business for a later door to position. residence_back_projection.note: A LATER HOME ADDRESS, READ BACKWARDS 8 YEARS. The street is not an 1835 reading: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 printed where this person lived in 1843, and this pass carries it back to the scene date because nothing in the 1835 corpus says where the house stood. What is claimed is the street FACE and nothing narrower — no lot, no roof, no door count, and no corner even where the volume prints one — and the grade is `reconstructed`, this dataset's word for a figure the reconstruction supplies rather than a source. Washington Street stands in 1835 under that name and in that place, and the entry prints it as this person's home. The volume narrows it further — it names La Salle Street — and clause R5 declines to take the point: a corner or a run between two crossings is a fact about the numbered grid of the 1840s, and a house moves more than a shopfront does. So the placement is the FACE and nothing narrower, and no roof is dealt. A home is carried back on a weaker argument than a shop is: a shopfront is capital sunk into one street's trade and a lodging is a month's rent, which is why this policy claims less than docs/ADDRESS-BACK-PROJECTION.md does from the same volume. The rule is docs/RESIDENCE-BACK-PROJECTION.md and the liberty is L223; a reader who thinks 8 years is too far to carry a house should read the grade as the disagreement being invited.
